meta.title: Who really said "If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Truman said it — but didn't coin it. In his 17 Dec 1952 Aero Club remarks he credited an old Jackson County Court colleague. Primary text verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen'?
meta.ogDescription: He used the line for years — then, in the speech that made it famous, said where he got it. The verified 1952 primary text, and why Wikiquote files it under Misattributed.

answer.label: Said by Truman — but not coined by him
answer.authorDates: 1884–1972 · 33rd President of the United States · popularizer, not originator
answer.sourceLine: Truman really did say it, and the best primary text is his Remarks at the Wright Memorial Dinner of the Aero Club of Washington, 17 December 1952. But in that very speech he introduced the line as “a saying that I used to hear from my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court” — he was quoting, not coining. Wikiquote files the saying under Misattributed for exactly that reason.

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Remarks at the Wright Memorial Dinner of the Aero Club of Washington
17 December 1952, 9:50 p.m. · Statler Hotel, Washington, D.C.
“my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court” (unnamed)
Harry S. Truman Presidential Library & Museum — transcript and audio (SR60-133)

source.excerpt: One of the results of this system is that it gives the President a good many hot potatoes to handle—but the President gets a lot of hot potatoes from every direction anyhow, and a man who can’t handle them has no business in that job. That makes me think of a saying that I used to hear from my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court. He said, “Harry, if you can’t stand the heat you better get out of the kitchen.” I’ll say that is absolutely true.
trail: Truman’s own words, 17 December 1952. He does not present the line as his: “That makes me think of a saying that I used to hear from my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court” — full transcript, Truman Library ↗, with an independent transcript at the American Presidency Project ↗.

He was already using it as a senator. A July 1942 item in the Soda Springs Sun called “If you don’t like the heat, get out of the kitchen” the favorite rejoinder of Senator Harry S. Truman when his war-contracts committee complained about his pace — phrases.org.uk ↗, which dates the item only to “July”; Barry Popik’s file dates the same syndicated column — Drew Pearson’s “Washington Merry-Go-Round” — to 12 July 1942 in the St. Petersburg Times ↗.

The specialists file it as not-his. Wikiquote places the saying under Misattributed: popularized rather than originated by Truman, credited to aide Harry H. Vaughan in Time (28 April 1952), and traced by Ralph Keyes to a Missouri colleague, Eugene “Buck” Purcell — Wikiquote ↗.

Truman said as much in print. In Mr. Citizen (1960) he wrote: “I used to have a saying that applies here, and I note that some people have picked it up” — then gave the modern wording — quoted at Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1952 phrasing is “you better get out of the kitchen.” The tighter imperative that circulates today is the form Truman printed in Mr. Citizen (1960), still framed there as a saying he had rather than one he made.

source.rightsNote: The passage quoted here is from remarks Truman delivered as President on 17 December 1952 and published in the Public Papers of the Presidents. Works prepared by an officer of the United States as part of official duties are not subject to copyright, so this text is free to reproduce. Note that Truman’s later book Mr. Citizen (1960), where the tighter modern wording appears, is a commercially published work and is not covered by that exemption — which is why the 1952 remarks are the text shown.

author.name: Harry S. Truman
author.heading: About Harry S. Truman
author.bio: Harry S. Truman was a Missouri farmer, failed haberdasher and Jackson County judge before he became a U.S. senator (1935–45) and then, on Franklin Roosevelt’s death, the 33rd President of the United States. His reputation rests as much on plain Missouri speech as on the decisions themselves — and this line is the purest example of it. He said it constantly, and he never claimed to have invented it: the phrasing he used in public was a borrowed county-courthouse saying he carried to the White House.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit — and who should
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote. It is a real saying that Truman said out loud, in public, more than once. The error is narrower and more interesting: the world credits him with writing a line he was openly repeating.

items.why: In the 1952 speech that fixed the phrase in American English, Truman prefaces it: “That makes me think of a saying that I used to hear from my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court.” He then quotes the man directly — Truman Library ↗.

Truman’s military aide was credited with the saying in Time on 28 April 1952, the attribution recorded by the Yale Book of Quotations — see Barry Popik’s citation file ↗. It stuck for a while, but nothing places the coinage with Vaughan.

Wikiquote ↗, citing Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier (2006), identifies Truman’s Missouri colleague as Purcell. Truman himself never gave the name, so this is Keyes’s identification rather than a documented self-attribution.

What Truman actually said in 1952 was “Harry, if you can’t stand the heat you better get out of the kitchen.” The crisp imperative everyone quotes is the form he printed himself in Mr. Citizen (1960), where he wrote that he “used to have a saying” and noted that people had picked it up — Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Truman used the saying from at least 1942 and made it famous in 1952 — but he presented it as borrowed, and on 17 December 1952 he pointed at the man he borrowed it from: read the passage ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to him
lead: Truman was president when the phrase entered general American speech, and he used it the way other people use a shrug — as a standing answer to anyone complaining about pressure. By July 1942, when he was still a senator running the war-contracts investigating committee, a syndicated column already called a version of it his “favorite rejoinder,” according to the citation file assembled by Barry Popik ↗.

What makes the 1952 Aero Club speech the right source is not just that the words are there — it is that Truman stops to say where he got them. He is talking about presidential decisions as “hot potatoes,” and the saying arrives as a piece of remembered courthouse wisdom, complete with the man who said it addressing him by his first name: “Harry.” The Truman Library holds the audio ↗.
detailsBody: Harry H. Vaughan. Truman’s military aide was credited with the line in Time on 28 April 1952 — the attribution that the Yale Book of Quotations records, per Popik’s file ↗. Vaughan was a famously quotable presence around Truman, which is enough to explain the confusion without making him the source.

Eugene ‘Buck’ Purcell. Wikiquote ↗, citing Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier (2006), identifies Truman’s Missouri colleague as Purcell. That fits Truman’s own description of an old friend from the Jackson County Court, but the identification belongs to Keyes — Truman never named the man in the speech.
context.pull: He did not coin it. He credited it — out loud, in the speech that made it famous.

schema.verdictNote: Truman said the line in public and is the reason it spread, but he introduced it as a saying he had heard from an old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court — popularizer, not originator. Ralph Keyes identifies that colleague as Eugene “Buck” Purcell; Truman never named him.

sourcesVerified.claim: Truman's 17 December 1952 remarks contain: "That makes me think of a saying that I used to hear from my old friend and colleague on the Jackson County Court. He said, 'Harry, if you can't stand the heat you better get out of the kitchen.' I'll say that is absolutely true."
The same passage, verbatim, appears in the American Presidency Project's transcript of the Wright Memorial Dinner remarks, confirming the text independently.

The Truman Library holds sound recording SR60-133, recording date 17 December 1952, whose description states that Truman uses the phrase 'if you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen', and that he spoke at 9:50 p.m. at the Statler Hotel in Washington.

Wikiquote lists the saying in its Misattributed section: not originated but popularized by Truman, credited to his aide Harry H. Vaughan in Time (28 April 1952), apparently originated with Missouri colleague Eugene 'Buck' Purcell per Ralph Keyes's The Quote Verifier (2006); and quotes Mr. Citizen (1960), p. 229, 'I used to have a saying that applies here, and I note that some people have picked it up, "If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen."'

Barry Popik's citation file dates the earliest entry to a 12 July 1942 Drew Pearson column (St. Petersburg Times) describing the line as Truman's favorite rejoinder, and records the 28 April 1952 Time attribution to Vaughan.

phrases.org.uk quotes the July 1942 Soda Springs Sun: 'Favorite rejoinder of Senator Harry S. Truman, when a member of his war contracts investigating committee objects to his strenuous pace: If you don't like the heat, get out of the kitchen.'
Wiktionary's etymology cites the July 1942 Soda Springs Sun report of the phrase as Senator Truman's favorite rejoinder.
